title: Cloud IAM Policy
summary: A cloud identity and access management policy is the machine-readable document that states which principal may perform which actions on which resources, and under what conditions, inside a cloud provider's control plane. In AWS an identity policy is a JSON document of allow and deny statements with an action, a resource, and sometimes a condition block, and access is granted only if some policy in the evaluation chain allows it; Azure expresses the same idea through role definitions assigned at a management group, subscription, resource group, or resource scope; Google Cloud binds a member to a role on a resource using allow-only grants. Two properties make these policies unusually dangerous to get wrong: every service enforces them at request time, so a single statement can expose data across many services, and identity policies can be attached to roles, users, or workloads, which means a careless trust relationship lets one principal assume another and inherit its permissions. The usual failure modes are wildcard actions or resources that grant far more than intended, service control policies or permission boundaries that nobody actually tested, unused access keys and forgotten service accounts that keep broad rights, and cross-account trust policies that let an external account take a role. The common mistake is writing a policy that looks narrow on paper without verifying effective permissions, because the result is the union of every attached policy and the resource policies applied by other accounts.

beginner.definition: A cloud identity and access management policy is a written rule inside a cloud service. It says who may use which service and what they may do with it. The cloud provider reads the rule before it allows an action. Rules can apply to a person, a group, or a program.
beginner.whyItMatters: In the cloud, one wrong rule can open a whole storage account to the world. Bad rules are a common cause of large data leaks. They also let an attacker who takes one account move into many others. Reading pages of rules by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. Clear, small rules limit the damage any single account can cause.
howItWorks: A person or program signs in and asks the cloud service to do something.
The cloud service collects every rule that applies to the identity making it.
Each rule names the actions allowed and the resources those actions may touch.
A condition may add limits, such as a required network or a time window.
If no rule allows the action, the request is refused and nothing happens.
Any deny rule wins, so one clear block can override many allows.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel where each key card is programmed for certain doors and hours. The card reader checks the card before the door opens. If the programmer sets a card for every room, the guest can enter anywhere. Nobody notices until something is missing. Careful programming is what keeps each guest in the right place.
takeaways: Grant the smallest set of actions on the smallest set of resources that still works.
Remember that the effective permission is the sum of every rule that applies.
Review old keys, roles, and trust rules, because they often keep old access alive.

objectives: Explain what a cloud identity and access management policy controls.
Describe how allow and deny statements are evaluated when a request is made.
Explain why effective permissions are the union of all attached policies.
Describe risks such as wildcard actions, unused keys, and over-broad trust relationships.
Explain how least privilege is applied and tested in a cloud environment.
Outline how conditions and permission boundaries narrow what a policy grants.
